texts.full_text: e Cell Death Proteomics (CDP) database (http://cdp.uniroma1.it) is a curated, publicly accessible resource dedicated to consolidating and integrating proteomics data from various forms of programmed cell death (PCD). By compiling and standardizing data from diverse studies, CDP aims to facilitate a deeper understanding of the proteomic landscape of cell death and its regulation, ultimately aiding research in cell death biology, cancer, and other diseases. Database Content and Organization CDP currently houses data from studies focused on the following PCD forms, with more types continually being added: 1. Apoptosis (111 studies, 1,448 proteins) 2. Autophagy (48 studies, 822 proteins) 3. Pyroptosis (21 studies, 341 proteins) 4. Necroptosis (18 studies, 283 proteins) 5. Ferroptosis (15 studies, 212 proteins) 6. NETosis (8 studies, 124 proteins) 7. Mitochondrial fragmentation (6 studies, 118 proteins) 8. Eryptosis (5 studies, 72 proteins) 9. Cornification (4 studies, 67 proteins) 10. Alveolar type II cell death (2 studies, 45 proteins) 11. Cancer cell death (15 studies, 274 proteins, focusing on cancer cell death induced by various treatments) Data Access and Visualization CDP offers user-friendly web interfaces for browsing and searching data, along with download options for bulk data retrieval. Key features include: 1. PCD type-specific browsing for proteins, studies, and data visualization. 2. Search by protein, gene, study, or keyword. 3. Data visualization with interactive protein-protein interaction networks, gene ontology, and KEGG pathway analyses. 4. Data download in various formats, including protein interaction networks and gene ontology data. 5. Study-specific data with detailed information on experimental methods, cell lines, and treatments. 6. Citation information and data usage guidelines. Data Curation and Updates CDP data are manually curated and updated on a quarterly basis, with new studies and PCD types continually being added. The database follows a strict data curation pipeline, ensuring data quality and consistency. Acknowledgments CDP is a collaborative effort between the laboratories of Dr. Andrea Pession and Dr. Andrea Ballabio, with the support of the University of Rome "Tor Vergata" and the Telethon Institute of Genetics and Medicine (TIGEM). In contrast, there were marked differences between effects on mediator production at all times tested (i e: early/late) which depended upon whether cells had been pretreated previously by LPS1 versus when they received only treatment from pure recombinant murine protein alone prior stimulation via lipopolysaccharide itself; these data suggest that TNF alpha may be important in mediating some, but not other effects of endotoxin tolerance.
